nameStory: The name 'ragwort' comes from the plant's deeply divided, ragged-looking leaves that reminded people of torn rags fluttering in the wind. Some of its more colorful folk names like 'stinking willie' and 'stinking nanny' refer to the plant's unpleasant, musty odor when crushed.
description: Ragwort is a yellow-flowered wildflower that looks like a cheerful daisy at first glance, but with a twist - it has deeply cut, ragged leaves that give it away. This European native typically grows 1-3 feet tall with bright golden-yellow flower clusters that bloom from summer into fall. It's an uncommon sight in New England, having been spotted only occasionally, but it's worth knowing since it can be toxic to livestock and is considered a noxious weed in some areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow daisy-like flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters, each flower head about half an inch across with narrow petals radiating from a yellow center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply cut and divided leaves that look almost lacy or ragged, dark green on top and often woolly underneath with a distinctive musty smell when crushed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright plant growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems forming a somewhat bushy appearance

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, fluffy seeds with white parachute-like bristles that blow away in the wind, similar to dandelion seeds but smaller

habitat: Look for ragwort in dry, open areas like fields, roadsides, waste places, and disturbed soils where it can establish without much competition. It prefers well-drained, often poor soils and full sun exposure. In New England, it's most likely to appear in coastal areas or along transportation corridors where seeds might arrive from other regions.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as rosettes close to the ground, showing their characteristic deeply divided shape. Young plants may be harder to spot among other emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with clusters of bright yellow flowers that are most noticeable from mid to late summer. The distinctive ragged leaves are fully developed and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue blooming into early fall, followed by fluffy seed heads that disperse in the wind. Leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level as an annual or biennial, leaving no above-ground parts to identify.

funFact: Despite being called 'stinking willie,' ragwort is actually a pollinator superhighway - it can support over 30 different species of insects, including some moths whose caterpillars can eat the toxic plant without harm and actually store the poison to make themselves unpalatable to predators!
confusionNotes: Ragwort's yellow daisy-like flowers can be confused with goldenrod, but goldenrod has completely different leaves - they're simple and uncut, not raggedy and deeply divided like ragwort's. Remember: 'Ragged leaves for ragwort, smooth leaves for goldenrod.'
contextualKnowledge: In the western United States, this same plant is commonly called 'tansy ragwort' even though it's not related to true tansy at all - the name comes from a superficial resemblance. This naming confusion can make identifying and researching the plant tricky when using different regional field guides.
compareHints: Ragwort differs from its relative dusty miller by having green leaves instead of silvery-white fuzzy ones, and yellow flowers instead of small, inconspicuous blooms. While dusty miller is commonly grown as an ornamental for its attractive silver foliage, ragwort is the weedy cousin that shows up uninvited with its ragged green leaves and bright yellow flower clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: This dusty miller differs from its relative common ragwort by having much more silvery, feltlike foliage and a compact garden habit, while ragwort has green leaves and grows as a weedy wildflower.
